summary:
KYMA – Hear the Earth.

KYMA is an interactive sonification app that translates NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into sound, so anyone can hear how our planet is changing. Starting with ocean temperature, Kyma maps the 0–32 °C range of a sea-surface map to [pitch / rhythm / timbre], letting people explore the data by listening rather than only by looking. It is designed from the start for blind and low-vision users, with screen reader support and a “Learn the sound” mode that teaches how to interpret what you hear. Ultimately, Kyma aims to make complex Earth science accessible, engaging and multisensory.

Project Details

A new scientific language: reading Earth data by ear

Earth observation reaches the public almost only as colour maps. A colour map is already a translation: a satellite measures a number, and a colour scale turns that number into a colour. KYMA adds a second translation that keeps the science intact. It turns each colour back into NASA’s measured value, then turns that value into sound, following a fixed set of rules. The result is a language of sounds for scientific data, which anyone can learn in minutes and use with or without sight.

The language has four rules:

  • Instrument = which variable. Each dataset has its own voice: a cello for sea surface temperature, a trumpet for active fires, a harp for vegetation, raindrops for rain, a choir for sea ice, an accordion for nitrogen dioxide.
  • Pitch = magnitude. Higher notes mean higher values.
  • Stereo = location. The sound moves from the left ear to the right ear as you move west to east across the map.
  • Silence = no data. KYMA never fills a gap with invented sound, because a missing measurement is information too.

The science behind it: from pixel to measured value

KYMA does not guess from how a colour looks. For every layer, we rebuilt the official colour scale from the legend NASA publishes with the visualization. Then we built a lookup table that turns each pixel’s colour back into the value that colour stands for. Each note is a reading of the data, not a decoration.

Getting this right meant solving real data-quality problems:

  • Masks. Sea ice has to be read only over the ocean, so we built an ocean mask from the vegetation layer and used it to stop the land from being read as ice.
  • Separating signal from background. On the rain layer, the colours of the base map could look like rain. A colour-saturation filter keeps only the real rain colours.
  • Calibrated bands. We set the nitrogen dioxide levels to match the scale’s own breakpoints (below 3, 3 to 5, above 5).
  • Knowing a dataset’s limits. Fire radiative power in megawatts gets inflated when the maps are reprojected and the pixels are combined. Instead of presenting a misleading number, we removed that measure. When a legend has no numbers, KYMA says “roughly” instead of inventing precision.
  • Validation. Anyone can upload a flat NASA map with its legend, and KYMA finds the colour bar automatically and reads the map. We checked these readings against our official layers: for nitrogen dioxide over Beijing, an uploaded map gave 5.7 against 6.0 from the official layer.

The sound design follows the same care. Values are mapped onto a 16-note pentatonic scale (C3 to C6), so differences in pitch are easy to hear and notes never clash. We balanced the volume of each instrument so that no variable sounds louder or more important than the others just because of its timbre.

Nine NASA datasets, one language

Sea surface temperature, aerosols, CO₂, night lights, vegetation (NDVI), rain and snow (IMERG), sea ice, active fires (VIIRS) and nitrogen dioxide. They come from visualizations by NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio and the Earth Information Center.

Three ways to use it, from first contact to analysis

  1. Listen. Drag across a map and hear the data under your finger, with the exact place and value shown beside it. Hearing works over time, so gradients, borders and sudden jumps stand out as you move: a warm current rises slowly, a fire front jumps.
  2. Learn. Nine missions, one per dataset. Each one teaches the sound of that variable and then sets a real reading task, such as “find the warmest water”.
  3. Play: Sound Detective. 10 worlds and 50 levels in which every question is answered from real NASA data: comparing regions, seasons and intensities.

Why it matters

  • For science communication: sound is a second channel for the same data. It shows patterns that people miss on a crowded colour map, and it helps them understand what a colour scale actually measures.
  • For accessibility: at least 2.2 billion people live with some form of vision impairment (WHO, 2026). For them, Earth science locked inside images is out of reach. KYMA opens it with nothing more than a browser and headphones (for better experience).
  • For NASA: KYMA reads the legends NASA already publishes, so existing visualizations can become audible without being remade.

Our vision: listening stations in museums and at the Earth Information Center, ready-made lessons for schools, and a general reader for any NASA map.

How it is creative

Most sonification projects turn one dataset into a fixed piece you can only listen to. KYMA is a reading system: one consistent language that works across nine variables and any compatible map, and that you can explore and question yourself. The game layer (an open solar system of 10 worlds, entered through a hyperspace jump) makes learning a scientific language something people want to do.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Sound: every instrument is made live in the browser with the Web Audio API.
  • Data reading: Canvas API, plus lookup tables rebuilt from each official NASA legend; automatic colour-bar detection for uploaded maps.
  • Data preparation: Python, to extract frames and legends from NASA SVS and EIC visualizations and build the land and ocean masks.
  • Testing: Playwright, for automated play-throughs of all 50 levels, all 9 missions and phone screens from 360 px wide.
  • SI help.
  • Delivery: one self-contained web page, in English and Spanish, with nothing to install.

Factors we considered

We considered faithfulness to the original measurement over looks; being open about each dataset’s limits; how easy the pitch is to hear and how comfortable it is to listen for a long time; and access on any device. Our next step is to test KYMA with blind and low-vision users and with Earth science educators, to measure how accurately people read data by ear.
